title: The Marriage and the Names
subtitle: Hosea 1
description: A prophet is told to marry his sermon, and his children's names preach it.
paragraphs: Hosea son of Beeri received the word of the LORD across the longest stretch of years of any prophet in this run of books. His first verse dates him by four kings of Judah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, and one of Israel, Jeroboam son of Jehoash, which means the voice that begins here in Jeroboam II's prosperous north, the same court Amos had just confronted, will still be speaking when that prosperity has rotted and the kingdom is nearing its end. Amos preached sermons. Jonah lived an argument. Hosea's assignment was stranger than either, because the first thing God gave him was not a message but a marriage: “Go, take a prostitute as your wife and have children of adultery, because this land is flagrantly prostituting itself by departing from the LORD.” The prophet's household was to be the illustration before it was anything else. Israel would not have to imagine its unfaithfulness as a picture. It could watch it being lived by the man sent to accuse it. So Hosea went and married Gomer, daughter of Diblaim, and the text records no protest, no negotiation, and nothing of Gomer's own words, because Gomer speaks no recorded word anywhere in this book. What the book records is the children, and what God did with their names.

The first child was a son, and his name was a place the story has already been: “Name him Jezreel, for soon I will bring the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and I will put an end to the kingdom of Israel.” Jezreel was the valley where Jehu had slaughtered the house of Ahab and seized the throne, the bloodbath the Kings account tells without flinching, and Jeroboam II sat on Jehu's throne as his great-great-grandson, the dynasty's fourth king. Every time the prophet called his boy in from the street, the sentence was spoken aloud in Israel: the blood of Jezreel is coming due on Jehu's house, and the kingdom itself has an end date. “And on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the Valley of Jezreel.” The bow, the nation's military strength, broken in the same valley that gave the child his name. A name in this book is never a label. It is an oracle small enough to be carried by a child.

The second child was a daughter, and her name cut deeper than geography: “Name her Lo-ruhamah, for I will no longer have compassion on the house of Israel, that I should ever forgive them.” Lo-ruhamah means No Compassion, mercy withdrawn, and the name would be spoken over this girl at every meal and market of her childhood. But inside the same naming, the text makes an exception that matters to the whole shape of the book, because Judah, the southern kingdom, is not folded into Israel's sentence: “Yet I will have compassion on the house of Judah, and I will save them”, and the manner of the saving is specified with care, “not by bow or sword or war, not by horses and cavalry, but by the LORD their God”. Israel will be ended by the instruments nations trust. Judah will be saved by none of them. The distinction stands in the first chapter and is never withdrawn: the prophet's war is with the north, and his own book will keep a door marked Judah open until its final chapter.

After the daughter was weaned, Gomer bore a second son, and the third name is the heaviest sentence in the chapter, the covenant itself read backwards: “Name him Lo-ammi, for you are not My people, and I am not your God.” Lo-ammi, Not My People. At Sinai God had bound Israel to Himself with almost these exact words as a promise; now the formula runs in reverse out of the same mouth, and a toddler carries it. Three children walk through this book's first chapter like three placards: the kingdom ended, compassion withdrawn, the covenant disowned. If the book closed at verse 9 it would be the bleakest opening in the prophets. It does not close there.

The chapter's last two verses turn the whole naming upside down, and they are quoted here in full because everything Hosea says afterward stands on them: “the number of the Israelites will be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or counted”. In the very place where the sentence was pronounced, the sentence will be reversed: where it was said to them, “You are not My people”, “they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’” “Then the people of Judah and of Israel will be gathered together, and they will appoint for themselves one leader, and will go up out of the land. For great will be the day of Jezreel.” Even the valley's name is redeemed in the promise: Jezreel, which means God scatters, also means God sows, and the book will end with God sowing His people in the land. The marriage and the names are the whole book in miniature, judgment stated in full and a reversal promised inside the same breath, and the next movement shows how both can be true at once, as God opens His case against the mother of these children, who is not Gomer. The mother in the lawsuit is Israel herself.

title: Plead with Your Mother
subtitle: Hosea 2
description: God pleads His case against Israel as a husband, and ends it with a betrothal.
paragraphs: Chapter two opens inside the family courtroom, and the reader has to hold the metaphor firmly to follow it: God is speaking of Israel as a wife, and of the Israelites as her children, and the children are the ones addressed first. Their task is an indictment of their own mother: “Rebuke your mother, rebuke her, for she is not My wife, and I am not her husband.” The grounds are stated as adultery carried on her face for all to see, and the alternative to repentance is stated without decoration: “I will strip her naked and expose her like the day of her birth. I will make her like a desert and turn her into a parched land, and I will let her die of thirst.” In the book's courtroom language this is the exposure of the nation, her glory removed, her land dried to desert, her children unpitied because they are children of the same adultery. The lawsuit is not a private quarrel. It is the covenant being prosecuted in the open, with the nation as the accused and her own prophets and children as the witnesses called to plead.

The defense Israel would have given is quoted in her own voice, and it is the voice of a woman keeping accounts: “I will go after my lovers, who give me bread and water, wool and linen, oil and drink.” The lovers are the Baals, the fertility gods of the land, and her testimony is that they pay. Bread, water, wool, flax, oil, drink, the whole subsistence of an agricultural nation, credited to the shrines. God's answer to her ledger is one verse of pure exposure: “she does not acknowledge that it was I who gave her grain, new wine, and oil, who lavished on her silver and gold”, and then where the silver and gold actually went, “which they crafted for Baal”. Every gift on her list had come from the husband she was leaving, and the gifts themselves had been melted down into the rivals' images. This is the engine of the whole book: Israel's sin is not chiefly rebellion but misattribution, a nation thanking the wrong giver for its bread, and Hosea's marriage stands behind the metaphor as its lived proof, a wife provided for by one man and crediting another.

So the husband acts, and his first act is not divorce but obstruction: “I will hedge up her path with thorns; I will enclose her with a wall, so she cannot find her way.” The path to the lovers gets fenced. “She will pursue her lovers but not catch them; she will seek them but not find them.” And the hedge is designed to produce a sentence, spoken by Israel herself when the pursuit finally exhausts her: “I will return to my first husband, for then I was better off than now.” It is not yet love; it is arithmetic, a woman comparing provisions. But the book treats even that cold calculation as a door. Before it opens, the gifts are reclaimed in sequence, each one named as his all along: “I will take back My grain in its time and My new wine in its season”, the wool and linen withdrawn, her lewdness exposed before the lovers who cannot rescue her, and the festival calendar on which the whole Baal religion ran shut down at a stroke: “I will put an end to all her exultation: her feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths”. The vines and fig trees she called her lovers' wages are made a thicket for wild beasts, and the chapter's prosecution rests on four words: “But Me she forgot,” declares the LORD.

Then, with no transition the reader is prepared for, the tone changes completely, and the change is the reason this chapter stands at the center of the book. The husband who hedged her path now speaks of winning her back, and his chosen ground is the wilderness, the very desert of the stripping sentence: “I will allure her and lead her to the wilderness, and speak to her tenderly.” There, in the emptiness where the lovers cannot follow, the gifts begin returning in a different order. Her vineyards are given back. And a place-name from Israel's darkest early story is picked up and reversed: God will “make the Valley of Achor into a gateway of hope”. Achor was the valley of trouble, where Achan's theft had brought defeat and death in Joshua's day; here the valley of trouble becomes hope's gate, and she will answer there as she did in her youth, “as in the day she came up out of Egypt”. Even the marriage's language is to be healed: “you will call Me ‘my Husband,’ and no longer call Me ‘my Master.’” The names of the Baals will be taken from her lips altogether, and in their place a covenant is made that reaches beyond the couple, with the beasts of the field and the birds of the air, war abolished from the land, and a people made to lie down in safety.

The chapter closes with the betrothal spoken three times, and the series has no warmer paragraph in this run of books: “So I will betroth you to Me forever; I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in loving devotion and compassion.” “I will betroth you in faithfulness, and you will know the LORD.” Then the whole ordered world answers in a chain, heaven responding to God and earth to heaven: “I will respond to the heavens, and they will respond to the earth”, the earth answering with grain and new wine and oil, and all of it answering to one name, Jezreel, the scattered valley now the sown field. And the last verse of the chapter gathers the three placard children from chapter one and reverses every name over them in a single sentence: “I will sow her as My own in the land, and I will have compassion on ‘No Compassion.’ I will say to those called ‘Not My People,’ ‘You are My people,’ and they will say, ‘You are my God.’” That is the promise. The book now turns back to the present tense, where the wife is still in another man's house, and the prophet is told to go and buy her.

title: Bought Back, and No Knowledge of God
subtitle: Hosea 3
description: Hosea buys back his wife, and the trial of the land opens on a missing knowledge.
paragraphs: Between the promise at the end of chapter two and the oracles that fill the rest of the book, one short chapter of action intervenes, the last scene of the prophet's marriage the book records. “Go show love to your wife again, though she is loved by another and is an adulteress. Love her as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods and love to offer raisin cakes to idols.” The wife is in another man's keeping now, and the love commanded is not described as a feeling recovered but as an errand run: Hosea goes and purchases her. The price is stated with a bookkeeper's plainness, and it is not a rich price: “So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley.” Part silver, part grain, the price of a person assembled out of what the prophet had. The text draws no attention to the humiliation of it. It simply records that the husband paid to recover the wife who had cost him everything, as the enacted picture of a God who loves a people busy loving other gods over their raisin cakes.

The terms Hosea sets are a season of waiting, for her and for him alike: “You must live with me for many days; you must not be promiscuous or belong to another, and I will do the same for you.” And then the chapter does what the names did in chapter one, it reads the prophet's household as the nation's future, in the text's own words: “the Israelites must live many days without king or prince, without sacrifice or sacred pillar, and without ephod or idol”. Everything Israel organizes its life around, throne and altar, true worship and false, is suspended for a long season in which the nation belongs fully to neither its lovers nor yet again to its God. The chapter's last sentence is the door out of the season, kept exactly as written: “the people of Israel will return and seek the LORD their God and David their king. They will come trembling to the LORD and to His goodness in the last days.” Return, trembling, goodness, and a king named David, spoken over a kingdom that will be kingless for many days first. With that, the marriage scenes end. Gomer does not appear again. The remaining eleven chapters are the voice of the husband in the metaphor, prosecuting His case, and chapter four opens the trial.

“Hear the word of the LORD, O children of Israel, for the LORD has a case against the people of the land”, and the indictment begins not with idolatry but with an absence, three missing things whose lack explains everything else: “There is no truth, no loving devotion, and no knowledge of God in the land!” What fills the vacuum is then listed like a police blotter of the whole society: “Cursing and lying, murder and stealing, and adultery are rampant; one act of bloodshed follows another.” The damage is not confined to people. In Hosea the land itself is a casualty of the moral weather, mourning and wasting: “the land mourns, and all who dwell in it will waste away”, and the wasting runs down the whole order of creation, beasts of the field, birds of the air, “even the fish of the sea disappear”. No other prophet in this run makes the fish of the sea a line item in a nation's indictment. In Hosea creation itself is called as evidence.

At the center of the case stands the charge the book is remembered for, and it is aimed at the teachers first: “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you as My priests.” The exchange is measured and exact. Knowledge rejected, priests rejected. “Since you have forgotten the law of your God, I will also forget your children.” A generation of children stands downstream of a priesthood that forgot, and the forgetting itself is punished by being forgotten. Nor does the guilt stay with the clergy; the chapter insists on the rot's symmetry: “And it shall be like people, like priest. I will punish both of them for their ways and repay them for their deeds.” They eat and are not satisfied, multiply their promiscuity and do not multiply; the appetites run and the fruit does not come, because a nation consulted wooden idols and divining rods instead. “My people consult their wooden idols, and their divining rods inform them. For a spirit of prostitution leads them astray”, and the sacrifices multiply on every pleasant hilltop, under oak and poplar and terebinth, shade being the whole of the theology.

The chapter's last movement refuses the easiest target. It declines to punish the daughters for a prostitution the men themselves practice openly: “For the men themselves go off with prostitutes and offer sacrifices with shrine prostitutes. So a people without understanding will come to ruin.” Judah is warned off Israel's road by name, Gilgal and Beth-aven marked as places not to journey to, and the nation is compared to livestock that will not be led: Israel “is as obstinate as a stubborn heifer”, and the shepherd's question hangs over her, “Can the LORD now shepherd them like lambs in an open meadow?” The chapter closes with the sentence the outline of this book flagged in advance, because it sounds like God giving up inside His own prosecution: “Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone!” Joined, welded, inseparable. Leave him alone is not the book's last word; eleven chapters stand against it, including a betrothal and a buy-back already told. But it is a real word in the trial, and the trial is only beginning, because a wind is already rising at the chapter's edge, wrapping them in its wings.

title: The Moth and the Morning Mist
subtitle: Hosea 5
description: A moth, a lion who withdraws, and a repentance song answered by morning mist.
paragraphs: Chapter five addresses the leadership by name and closes every exit in sequence. “Hear this, O priests! Take heed, O house of Israel! Give ear, O royal house!” The judgment is against all three because the shepherds have become the trap: “you have been a snare at Mizpah, a net spread out on Tabor”, hunting gear set on the two great heights, where the people came expecting God. Underneath the public corruption sits the book's recurring diagnosis, the reason return itself has become impossible for them: “Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God, for a spirit of prostitution is within them, and they do not know the LORD.” Not a knowledge they lost in an argument. A knowledge that was never in them, crowded out from inside. Israel's arrogance testifies against her like a witness who needs no cross-examination, and when she comes with flocks and herds to seek the LORD in the formal way, the seeking fails for the simplest reason in the book: “They go with their flocks and herds to seek the LORD, but they do not find Him; He has withdrawn Himself from them.”

Judah is not allowed to watch from a safe distance this time. Her princes are indicted under an image every farmer in the audience understood as theft: “The princes of Judah are like those who move boundary stones; I will pour out My fury upon them like water.” To move a boundary stone was to steal a neighbor's inheritance a furrow at a time, and God promises fury poured like the element Judah cannot dam. Then the chapter gives its two animal sentences, the small one and the great one. The small one first, judgment as slow decay rather than invasion: “I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like decay to the house of Judah.” A moth does not besiege a garment; it ruins it quietly from inside the folds, and rot does not strike a beam, it eats until the beam fails under ordinary weight. When Ephraim finally felt his sickness, he ran to the era's great power for the cure, and the text's verdict on the errand is four words of medical finality: “But he cannot cure you or heal your wound.” Assyria can conquer a wound. It cannot close one.

Then the great animal replaces the small one, and the lion of Amos's roar stands in Hosea's chapter doing the opposite of presiding. In God's own words, He will “tear them to pieces and then go away. I will carry them off where no one can rescue them.” And in the oracle's last line the withdrawal itself is given a purpose and a limit: “Then I will return to My place until they admit their guilt and seek My face; in their affliction they will earnestly seek Me.” Until. The lion's departure is not abandonment as an end. It is abandonment as a strategy, a God who goes back to His place and waits for the affliction to do what the prophets could not. Chapter six opens with the sound the waiting was designed to produce. It is Israel speaking now, the people singing their repentance, and the narration of this book keeps their words in their mouths, because what God says next depends on whose voice this is: “Come, let us return to the LORD. For He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us; He has wounded us, but He will bind up our wounds.” “After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence.”

The song is beautiful, and it is glib. It schedules the resurrection for the third day the way a man books a room; it assumes the torn people's healing is a mechanism that affliction automatically triggers. Its best line is its aspiration: “let us press on to know the LORD. As surely as the sun rises, He will appear; He will come to us like the rain, like the spring showers that water the earth.” Knowledge of the LORD, the very thing chapter four said the land had none of, is here claimed as a program. God's answer takes the song apart at its one accurate seam: “What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? What shall I do with you, O Judah? For your loyalty is like a morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes.” Morning mist is real water. It is simply gone by the time the field needs it. The loyalty was not faked; it was weather. And against the whole apparatus of song and sacrifice the answer sets the book's thesis, the line this series' readers will carry out of Hosea if they carry only one: “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.”

The case then returns to evidence. The covenant has been broken from the beginning of the line: “they, like Adam, have transgressed the covenant”. Gilead is a city of evildoers tracked with bloody footprints; a band of priests murders travelers on the Shechem road, clergy as highwaymen, the worst single image in the chapter and the one given without elaboration, as the text gives it. Ephraim's prostitution and Israel's defilement are named as the horrible thing seen in the house of Israel, and the episode closes where the chapter closes, on the one line of the harvest that points past the wreckage, a promise made to the kingdom that has so far only been warned: “for you, O Judah, a harvest is appointed”, a harvest appointed “when I restore My people from captivity”. Judah's harvest and Israel's restoration are tied in one sentence, and the book turns back north, to a court baking its plots in an oven.

title: The Whirlwind
subtitle: Hosea 7
description: An oven of kings, a silly dove between empires, and the law of the whirlwind.
paragraphs: Chapters seven and eight are the book's portrait of a kingdom rotting at the center, drawn mostly in kitchen and barnyard images that turn sinister as they accumulate. The first thing said of the court is that its evil is not hidden from the one Person it needed to hide from: “they fail to consider in their hearts that I remember all their evil. Now their deeds are all around them; they are before My face.” The court's shared metaphor is an oven. The princes prepare their hearts like a baker's oven, anger smoldering all night while they lie in wait, blazing by morning; the king joins hands with mockers, inflamed with wine on his own feast day; and the result is a dynasty consuming itself: “All of them are hot as an oven, and they devour their rulers. All their kings fall; not one of them calls upon Me.” Hosea lived under the last kings of Israel, a throne changing hands by assassination in his own lifetime, and the book's diagnosis of the coups is a baker's: the heat was banked long before it flamed, and in all the palace fires, not one king called on God.

Ephraim abroad gets the book's saddest comic images. “Ephraim mixes with the nations; Ephraim is an unturned cake.” A cake on hot stones, baked black on one side and raw dough on the other, never flipped: that is the nation's strength and judgment in one picture, half done and wholly ruined. The decay is measurable and unmeasured by the one decaying: “Foreigners consume his strength, but he does not notice. Even his hair is streaked with gray, but he does not know.” A man going gray without ever seeing a mirror. And his foreign policy, the shuttle between the two great powers that the Kings account records as policy, is rendered as a bird's panic: Ephraim “has become like a silly, senseless dove”, “calling out to Egypt, then turning to Assyria”, fluttering between the two empires that will between them end him. The dove image curdles instantly into the fowler's trade: “As they go, I will spread My net over them; I will bring them down like birds of the air.” The chapter closes on the nation's speech defect, the root of the faulty aim: “They turn, but not to the Most High; they are like a faulty bow”, a bow that cannot shoot straight because its whole curve is wrong, and their leaders' cursing tongues earn them ridicule in Egypt, of all places, the house of slavery turned audience.

Chapter eight opens with the alarm trumpet and the book's most quoted sentence about claims to know God: “Put the ram’s horn to your lips! An eagle looms over the house of the LORD, because the people have transgressed My covenant and rebelled against My law.” Israel's response to the eagle is a confession of faith, cried out in the crisis: “O our God, we know You!” The book has spent four chapters establishing that the land has no knowledge of God, and the cry is answered by the record: good rejected, an enemy in pursuit, kings and princes set up without God's appointment, and the wealth of the nation cast into the thing that replaced Him: “He has rejected your calf, O Samaria.” The calf at Bethel, Jeroboam's altar-piece from the founding of the kingdom, is addressed as Samaria's own possession and God's settled rejection, and its manufacture is its refutation: “a craftsman made it, and it is not God. It will be broken to pieces, that calf of Samaria.” A god with a maker has an ending, and the ending is pieces.

Then comes the law of the harvest the episode is named for, stated once and governing everything after it: “they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind”. Wind is nothing, seed that weighs nothing and feeds no one; the whirlwind is the same element at destructive scale, the nothing returning as a storm. The standing grain with no head, the flour that never comes, the produce swallowed by foreigners, all of it unfolds from that one ratio. “Israel is swallowed up! Now they are among the nations like a worthless vessel.” And the diplomatic farce completes its circuit: “they have gone up to Assyria like a wild donkey on its own. Ephraim has hired lovers.” A wild ass alone in the desert is the picture of the foreign policy, stubborn, solitary, and paying for what it calls alliance. Even the law becomes evidence: “Though I wrote for them the great things of My law, they regarded them as something strange.” The written gift of God filed as foreign literature by His own people.

The chapter ends with the sentence that reverses the founding story of the nation, and the book places it without underlining, which makes it land harder: “They will return to Egypt.” Not as slaves in chains this time, though the Assyrian exile will carry them past Egypt's orbit soon enough in the story's history; return to Egypt stands in Hosea as the anti-exodus, the undoing of the one act by which Israel knew God at all. Palaces built, cities fortified, Maker forgotten: “I will send fire upon their cities, and it will consume their citadels.” The whirlwind is still rising. Ahead of it stands a prophet the nation calls a fool, watching the roads to the threshing floor, and a vine that has grown so luxuriant it can no longer see its own altars for the fruit.

title: The Watchman and the Vine
subtitle: Hosea 9
description: The watchman is called a fool, and the luxuriant vine meets the plow.
paragraphs: Chapter nine forbids the nation its joy, because the joy itself has been hired out: “Do not rejoice, O Israel, with exultation like the nations, for you have played the harlot against your God”. The harvest festivals at the threshing floor, where Israel celebrated the gifts chapter two said she credited to her lovers, are appointed to fail: the floor and the winepress will not feed them, the new wine will let them down. Exile is described as a diet before it is described as a journey: “They will not remain in the land of the LORD; Ephraim will return to Egypt and eat unclean food in Assyria.” Bread in the land of exile becomes the bread of mourners, defiling everyone who eats it, acceptable nowhere near the house of the LORD. And the geography of the end is given a burial address: “Egypt will gather them and Memphis will bury them.” Silver treasured up for the shrines will be inherited by thistles, thorns will run through their tents, and the question hangs over the appointed feast day itself, what will you do when the day comes and there is nothing and no one left to celebrate with.

In the middle of the chapter stands the book's portrait of the prophet's office in a nation that no longer wants one. “The days of punishment have come; the days of retribution have arrived”, and the nation's review of its watchman is contempt: “The prophet is called a fool, and the inspired man insane”. Hosea's own description of the office follows, and it is a picture of occupational futility: “The prophet is Ephraim’s watchman, along with my God, yet the snare of the fowler lies on all his paths.” A watchman whose every path is trapped, hostility waiting for him even in the house of his God. The ground of the hostility is then dug down to the nation's deepest archaeological layer: “They have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah”, Gibeah, where Benjamin's outrage in the days of the judges nearly erased a tribe and whose story this series told in Judges 19-21. Hosea's audience is told that the corruption is not new. It is ancestral, continuous, and remembered.

Against that depth of corruption the chapter sets the depth of the original love, in the book's most tender backward look: “I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness. I saw your fathers as the firstfruits of the fig tree in its first season.” Grapes in a desert, the first fig of the season, delight language, a finder's joy. Then the sentence turns on its hinge: “they went to Baal-peor, and consecrated themselves to Shame; so they became as detestable as the thing they loved”. Baal-peor, the plague at Peor in the wilderness generation, is named as the moment the found delight consecrated itself to the thing called Shame, and the law of the whole tragedy is stated in the result: people become as detestable as what they love. Worship is formation. The consequence falls on the nurseries of the nation, answering chapter one's children with a terrible symmetry: “Ephraim’s glory will fly away like a bird, with no birth, no pregnancy, and no conception.” At Gilgal the root of it is located and the love itself renounced in words no reader of the marriage chapters can hear as anything but agony: “there I hated them. I will drive them from My house for the wickedness of their deeds. I will no longer love them”. Struck down, root withered, fruitless, and the chapter's last line sends them out under the oldest curse in Israel's memory: “they shall be wanderers among the nations”. Cain's sentence, become a nation's address.

Chapter ten opens with the nation's other self-portrait, the vine: “Israel was a luxuriant vine, yielding fruit for himself. The more his fruit increased, the more he increased the altars.” Prosperity in Hosea is never neutral; it is building material, and Israel builds altars with it, improving the sacred pillars as the harvests improve, a direct proportion between God's blessing and Israel's idolatry. The sentence on the whole installation is dismantling: “The LORD will break down their altars and demolish their sacred pillars.” The king question collapses next. The nation that cried for kings hears its own future voice: “We have no king, for we do not revere the LORD.” And the calf of Beth-aven, Bethel renamed by Hosea as the house of wickedness, is given a funeral in advance: its people and its idolatrous priests will mourn it as it is carried off as tribute, “it will be carried to Assyria as tribute to the great king”. Samaria's god, freighted to the empire. Samaria herself follows like a twig on the water's surface, and the high places fill with the thorns that inherited the silver in chapter nine, until the people of the hills beg the landscape itself for burial, asking the mountains to cover them and the hills to fall on them.

The last movement of the episode plows. Ephraim is recast one final time, from vine to farm animal, and the image is unexpectedly gentle: “Ephraim is a well-trained heifer that loves to thresh; but I will place a yoke on her fair neck.” Threshing was the easy work, the animal walking the grain with its mouth free to eat; the yoke means the hard ground now, harness and plow, Judah and Jacob called to the same field. And out of the yoke comes the book's great farming command, the positive sentence toward which the whole plowing metaphor has been driving: “Sow for yourselves righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion; break up your unplowed ground. For it is time to seek the LORD until He comes and sends righteousness upon you like rain.” Unplowed ground, fallow and crusted, is the book's last picture of the nation's heart before its ending: breakable, but only by being broken. The alternative harvest is stated in the same furrow: “You have plowed wickedness and reaped injustice; you have eaten the fruit of lies.” And the reaping arrives as it did at Beth-arbel, where Shalman devastated the town in the day of battle, “when mothers were dashed to pieces along with their children”, the war atrocity stated in the text's own words and left there, as the text leaves it. The episode closes at dawn, as the chapter does: “When the day dawns, the king of Israel will be utterly cut off.” Behind the cut-off king stands a child once found like grapes in a wilderness. The next movement goes back to him, and to the Father who found him.

title: When Israel Was a Child
subtitle: Hosea 11
description: God remembers teaching His child to walk, and His heart turns within Him.
paragraphs: Chapter eleven changes the book's governing picture. For ten chapters Israel has been the unfaithful wife; now, without announcement, she is a child, and God speaks as a father remembering the nursery. “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son.” The exodus is retold as an adoption, and its sadness is in the arithmetic of response: “the more I called Israel, the farther they departed from Me”. The more calling, the more departing, a proportion no parent in the audience needed explained. Against the Baals and the carved images the chapter sets its inventory of tenderness, the most physical description of God's care in the prophets: “It was I who taught Ephraim to walk, taking them by the arms, but they never realized that it was I who healed them.” “I led them with cords of kindness, with ropes of love; I lifted the yoke from their necks and bent down to feed them.” Hands under the arms of a toddler. A yoke lifted off a neck by the one who fed the animal bending down. The images are parental to the point of embarrassment, and the book sets them deliberately where they stand, before the sentence, so the sentence lands on a reader who has just been shown the father's hands.

The sentence is not withdrawn. “My people are bent on turning from Me.” Bent, curved away by constitution, and the sword is already drawn in the oracle: “A sword will flash through their cities; it will destroy the bars of their gates and consume them in their own plans.” Egypt and Assyria wait at the borders of the paragraph as the geography of refusal. Everything the previous ten chapters built says the next line should be the execution. Instead the book arrives at the passage this whole episode exists to carry, God's argument with Himself, conducted in the open, in questions He answers by refusing them: “How could I give you up, O Ephraim? How could I surrender you, O Israel? How could I make you like Admah? How could I treat you like Zeboiim? My heart is turned within Me; My compassion is stirred!” Admah and Zeboiim were the small cities swept away with Sodom and Gomorrah in Genesis, total-loss names, and God declines the comparison in the act of speaking it. His heart turns over inside Him; the compassion is not a policy but a convulsion. Hosea's audience had heard Amos's God roar and swear He would never forget a deed. Hosea's God now says the anger will not be executed in full, and gives the reason as a statement about what kind of being He is: “I will not execute the full fury of My anger; I will not destroy Ephraim again.” “For I am God and not man”, “the Holy One among you”, “and I will not come in wrath”. A human husband, a human father, a human king would finish it. The Holy One announces that His holiness is precisely why He will not.

The sound that follows is the series' oldest prophetic sound turned inside out. In Amos, the lion's roar from Zion was the signal that judgment could not be recalled. Here the roar is a father's call home: “He will roar like a lion. When He roars, His children will come trembling from the west.” “They will come trembling like birds from Egypt and like doves from the land of Assyria. Then I will settle them in their homes”. The dove of chapter seven, silly and senseless between the empires, returns as the child coming home trembling at the roar. Trembling is the book's word for the right response all along; the bought-back wife's nation was to come trembling to the LORD and to His goodness, and here the trembling is the children's, on the road home. Chapter eleven closes with the sentence still standing beside the mercy, because the book never lets one cancel the other: Ephraim surrounds God with lies even while Judah still walks with Him. The father's heart has been shown. The son has not yet turned.

Chapter twelve argues the case out of the family album, and its subject is the nation's grandfather. “In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel, and in his vigor he wrestled with God.” Jacob is Hosea's mirror for Ephraim: grasping from birth, striving with the angel at the river, and prevailing in the strangest way the patriarchal stories know, by holding on and weeping: “he struggled with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought His favor; he found Him at Bethel and spoke with Him there”. Bethel, the house of God where Ephraim's calf now stands, was first the place where the heel-grasper met God and was remade, and Hosea sets the two Bethels side by side without comment, the altar of the wrestling and the altar of the calf. Out of the history comes the book's practical command, addressed to Jacob's descendants in Jacob's own grammar of return: “But you must return to your God; maintain love and justice, and always wait on your God.” Around the command the chapter spreads the evidence of the alternative: “A merchant loves to defraud with dishonest scales in his hands”, Ephraim boasting that his wealth proves his innocence, the altars of Gilgal destined to be heaps of stones in furrows.

The episode closes with the two journeys of Jacob set against each other, because Hosea's last word about the grandfather is not the wrestling but the wage work: “Jacob fled to the land of Aram and Israel worked for a wife”, “for a wife he tended sheep”. The father of the nation earned his bride by shepherding another man's flocks in a foreign land, and the prophet who tells it had himself just bought back a wife with silver and barley; the book does not underline the rhyme, it simply lets the two bride-prices stand chapters apart. And against Jacob the servant stands the other instrument of the nation's making, the office Hosea himself holds: “by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved”. By a prophet they were brought up; by prophets they were kept; and the prophet now speaking is the last keeper the north will be offered. Ahead lies the final indictment, the bear robbed of her cubs and the ransoming questions at the edge of Sheol, and then, at the very end of the book, a door standing open with words put in the returning people's mouths.

title: I Will Heal Their Apostasy
subtitle: Hosea 13
description: The final indictment, the ransom questions at Sheol's edge, and love given freely.
paragraphs: The final indictment opens with a memory of consequence: “When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he was exalted in Israel. But he incurred guilt through Baal, and he died.” Once, the tribe's word made men tremble; the Baal guilt ended the authority and the man together. The sinning has since industrialized: cast images skillfully made from their silver, craftsmen's work worshiped as gods, and the report God files about the worshipers' own reputation is the chapter's coldest line, the words people say of them: “They offer human sacrifice and kiss the calves!” Human sacrifice and calf-kissing in one sentence, the depths and the absurdity filed together. The sentence pronounced over all of it is evanescence, the morning-mist image of chapter six returned no longer as a description of their loyalty but as the measure of their existence: “they will be like the morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes, like chaff blown from a threshing floor, like smoke through an open window”. Four things that cannot be gathered back. The nation that would not be sown as seed will be scattered as chaff, and the book's first valley-name hangs over the contrast.

Against the mist stands the memory the indictment refuses to drop: “I am the LORD your God ever since the land of Egypt; you know no God but Me, for there is no Savior besides Me.” “I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of drought.” Knew, in the wilderness, the verb of intimate care, and the tragedy of the book compressed into one agricultural cycle: “When they had pasture, they became satisfied; when they were satisfied, their hearts became proud, and as a result they forgot Me.” Pasture, satisfaction, pride, forgetting. The gifts that were supposed to bind the wife to the husband fattened her for the lovers, and the God who knew her in the drought announces what He becomes to the nation that forgot Him in the plenty: not a stranger, something worse, a hunter who knows her paths: “like a leopard I will lurk by the path”. “Like a bear robbed of her cubs I will attack them, and I will tear open their chests.” The robbed bear is the most violent animal in the prophets, maternal fury turned predator, and the book does not flinch from putting the image in God's mouth in the book where His heart turned over inside Him. Both portraits stand. Hosea does not reconcile them; he sets them in the same book and lets the last chapter answer which one has the future.

The indictment closes through the monarchy and the maternity ward, the nation's two bids for a future. The king experiment is filed in one sentence of divine irony: “in My anger I gave you a king, and in My wrath I took him away”. Asked for in anger, removed in wrath, the whole institution bracketed by the two angers. And birth itself, the nation's other road forward, fails at the threshold: “he is an unwise son. When the time arrives, he fails to present himself at the opening of the womb.” A child who will not be born, a nation stuck at its own delivery. Then, at the very edge of the indictment, Hosea places the two most astonishing sentences in the chapter, the ransoming questions flung at the grave itself: “I will ransom them from the power of Sheol; I will redeem them from Death. Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting? Compassion is hidden from My eyes.” The taunt at Death is real and quoted exactly as the book gives it, and the oracle does not soften what follows it: the compassion hidden, the east wind already rising: “an east wind will come”, “a wind from the LORD rising up from the desert. His fountain will fail, and his spring will run dry.” The treasury plundered of every precious thing, and Samaria's bearing of her guilt in the book's hardest verse, in the text's own terms, neither elaborated nor looked away from: “their little ones will be dashed to pieces, and their pregnant women ripped open”. The whirlwind sown in chapter eight finishes its reaping there. And then the book does the thing no reader of the indictment expects. It opens a door.

Chapter fourteen is nine verses long and contains the whole future of the series' argument. It begins with the call the entire book has been circling: “Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God, for you have stumbled by your iniquity.” And because this nation has proven for fourteen chapters that it cannot even repent without being scripted, God scripts the repentance, putting the words in their mouths as a father teaches a child an apology: “Bring your confessions and return to the LORD.” The confession itself is given to them to say: “Take away all our iniquity and receive us graciously, that we may present the fruit of our lips.” “Assyria will not save us, nor will we ride on horses.” Never again Our gods to the work of their hands, and the ground of the whole appeal is the character of the one addressed: “For in You the fatherless find compassion.” The orphans of Lo-ammi's generation are told to come home on the strength of what God is to the fatherless. And the answer comes back in the sentence this episode is named for, the freest sentence in the book: “I will heal their apostasy; I will freely love them, for My anger has turned away from them.” Freely. The wife was bought back for fifteen shekels and barley; the love that receives her is priced at nothing, given first, before she has proven a single day of faithfulness.

The closing blessings reverse the book's whole image system in order. The morning mist and vanishing dew of chapters six and thirteen are answered by dew that stays: “I will be like the dew to Israel; he will blossom like the lily and take root like the cedars of Lebanon.” Root and blossom, the tree's splendor and the vine's fruitfulness, the luxuriant vine of chapter ten healed of its altars: “They will return and dwell in his shade; they will grow grain and blossom like the vine.” The lovers' economy of bread and oil and drink is replaced by an agriculture whose fruitfulness has one source, stated in the book's last exchange between God and Ephraim: “O Ephraim, what have I to do anymore with idols? It is I who answer and watch over him. I am like a flourishing cypress; your fruit comes from Me.” Then the book closes its own cover with an epilogue addressed past Israel entirely, to whoever is reading: “Whoever is wise, let him understand these things; whoever is discerning, let him know them. For the ways of the LORD are right, and the righteous walk in them but the rebellious stumble in them.” Same road, two walkings. Hosea's book ends there, the prophet who married his sermon stepping back, and leaving the ways of the LORD open in front of the reader.
